description: Multi-dimensional adversarial review of a diff or capability: correctness, security, and spec compliance, with every finding adversarially verified before it is reported.

args.scope: Phase 7 global release review of the backend (release-review-api), part d: tools/, Flyway migrations and resources, compose files, pom.xml
args.headRef: HEAD -- tools src/main/resources compose.yaml compose.e2e.yaml pom.xml
args.focus: This is the once-per-release whole-history review; slice reviews already happened per slice, so prioritise CROSS-MODULE and cross-slice defects. This run covers ONLY: tools, src/main/resources, compose.yaml, compose.e2e.yaml, pom.xml (read other modules only for context at call sites). Requirements: contract/docs/requirements.md; ownership table in contract/docs/mvp-capability-plan.md; API in contract/api/openapi.yaml. Check especially: answer keys leaking to child endpoints before reveal (FR-27, NFR-1); admin endpoints reachable without the admin; any user input producing a raw 500 or driver internals (RFC 7807 required); UNPARSEABLE consuming an attempt (FR-22); attempts persisted immediately (FR-31); XP ledger never reduced (FR-38); Europe/Prague week boundaries in stats; module boundaries (Spring Modulith); migrations append-only and consistent with entities; concurrency (double submit, races on attempts/XP); path traversal / upload limits in storage; no secrets committed; tools never addressing the owner's compose project 'doucko'. Skip tests unless they mask a defect.

findings.title: Attempt log and problem reports are 'append-only' only by comment; no DB guard unlike xp_award
findings.evidence: The header says 'Rows are only ever inserted: the attempt log is append-only (FR-42, OQ-20)', but attempt, opened_hint and problem_report get no UPDATE/DELETE trigger. V5 and V6 add such a trigger for xp_award and attempt_reevaluation. The attempt table is the FR-31/FR-42 evidence base, so any stray UPDATE would rewrite history without the database objecting.
findings.suggestion: Add a new migration with a BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE refusal trigger for attempt (and opened_hint), and a statement-level BEFORE TRUNCATE trigger for xp_award, attempt and attempt_reevaluation. Do not edit V4 itself.

findings.title: xp_award append-only trigger does not block TRUNCATE
findings.evidence: The trigger is declared 'BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE ... FOR EACH ROW'. Row-level triggers do not fire on TRUNCATE, so 'TRUNCATE xp_award' wipes the whole ledger and bypasses the FR-38 'XP is never lost' guard. The same applies to attempt_reevaluation in V6.
findings.suggestion: Add a statement-level BEFORE TRUNCATE trigger using the same refusal function, in a new migration.

findings.title: Backup/restore cover only the database, so uploaded PDFs and images can be lost or orphaned (NFR-10)
findings.evidence: pg_dump captures source.storage_key and task_image.storage_key, but the files live on the doucko-storage volume, which neither backup nor restore touches (restore.mjs only prints a notice). After a restore onto a fresh volume, rows point at missing files. The task images and source PDFs of an authored workbook would then fail to load, and the operator has no tool to recover them.
findings.suggestion: Archive the storage volume alongside the dump (tar from inside the backend container, or a volume copy) and restore it together. Or add a startup/admin consistency check that reports storage keys with no file.

findings.title: Restore replaces the schema while the backend keeps serving and writing
findings.evidence: The restore runs 'DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE' and replays the dump in one transaction without stopping the backend. A child attempt or XP award committed between the safety backup and the schema swap is silently discarded. Requests during the swap block on locks or hit a briefly empty schema. This is the data-loss window FR-31 and FR-38 forbid.
findings.suggestion: Stop the backend container before the swap ('docker compose stop backend') and start it afterwards, which also gives Flyway its migration run. Alternatively document and enforce that the stack is idle.

findings.title: practice_run cascade-deletes with a mission while attempt/opened_hint intentionally have no mission FK
findings.evidence: 'mission_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES mission (id) ON DELETE CASCADE' on practice_run removes run history when a mission is deleted. The same file says the log 'outlives later mission edits' and gives attempt.mission_id no FK. After a mission delete, replay-scope attempts remain whose scope (the run id) no longer resolves to any practice_run row.
findings.suggestion: Make the behaviour consistent: either RESTRICT the mission delete once runs exist (as done for task_id), or have stats treat scopes with no run as orphaned. Do this in a new migration.

findings.title: Plain 'docker compose up' bypasses the NFR-2 bind guard; DOUCKO_BIND_ADDRESS is not validated by compose
findings.evidence: The port mapping is '${DOUCKO_BIND_ADDRESS:-127.0.0.1}:8081:80'. An empty value (the .env.example placeholder) or 0.0.0.0 publishes the app on all interfaces if the operator runs 'docker compose up' directly. The header comment admits the guard lives only in tools/stack.mjs. The backend and its admin API are then reachable from outside the LAN, with only the admin password between them.
findings.suggestion: Add a compose-level guard, for example a required form '${DOUCKO_BIND_ADDRESS:?...}' with a documented 127.0.0.1 default in .env.example. Or add a backend startup warning/refusal, so the guard does not depend on the wrapper script.

findings.title: Session timeout/idle and backend healthcheck rely on image tooling not verified (wget in jre-alpine)
findings.evidence: The backend healthcheck runs 'wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/actuator/health | grep -q UP'. The runtime image is eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine, where wget is the busybox applet and 'localhost' may resolve to ::1 first. If it fails, 'up --wait' and the frontend's depends_on service_healthy never succeed, and restore.mjs reports the backend as unhealthy.
findings.suggestion: Use 127.0.0.1 explicitly in the healthcheck URL, and verify it against the built image in an IT or in the e2e-stack proof.

findings.title: NFR-2 bind guard is bypassable with plain `docker compose up`
findings.evidence: The frontend port is `${DOUCKO_BIND_ADDRESS:-127.0.0.1}:8081:80`. The only check that the address is loopback or RFC 1918 lives in `tools/stack.mjs` (`npm run stack:up`). If the owner or a script sets `DOUCKO_BIND_ADDRESS=0.0.0.0` in .env and runs `docker compose up` directly, the child surface and the admin login are published on every interface. Anyone on the network, or on the internet behind a port-forward, could then reach the admin login. compose.yaml says so in a comment, but nothing enforces it.
findings.suggestion: Make the safe default hard to override. For example, reject non-private values with a compose interpolation pattern, or add a startup check in the nginx or backend image that refuses a public Host. Alternatively, document that `stack:up` is the only supported entry point and make `down`, `ps` and `restore` use the same guarded path.

findings.title: Restore runs against a live backend with no write quiesce
findings.evidence: The restore does `DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE` inside the db container while the backend keeps serving. The backend is only restarted afterwards, and only when the schema is behind. A child attempt or XP write that lands between the safety backup and the drop is lost silently, since the append-only ledger never records it. Open pool connections and Hibernate state also point at a replaced schema until a restart. In the common case where the restored schema equals the target, no restart happens at all.
findings.suggestion: Stop the backend before the drop (`compose stop backend`) and start it again afterwards, always. That also makes Flyway run unconditionally and clears the pool state. Alternatively, refuse to restore while the backend container is running.

findings.title: Storage volume is not covered by backup although DB rows reference it by storage_key
findings.evidence: `source.storage_key` and `task_image.storage_key` (V2) point at files on the `doucko-storage` volume. `tools/backup.mjs` dumps only the database, and `restore.mjs` prints a warning about this. After a disk loss or a restore on a fresh volume, published tasks keep their rows but their PDFs and images are gone. This is a data-integrity gap, not an exploit.
findings.suggestion: Have backup also archive the storage volume (for example `tar` through `docker compose exec`, into the same owner-only directory). Alternatively, add a startup or admin consistency check that reports rows whose files are missing.

findings.title: DB-level append-only guard on xp_award and attempt_reevaluation does not cover TRUNCATE; attempt and opened_hint have no guard
findings.evidence: The triggers are `BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE ... FOR EACH ROW`. `TRUNCATE xp_award` and `TRUNCATE attempt_reevaluation` bypass them. The `attempt` log (FR-31, FR-42) is described as append-only, but V4 has no trigger, so an UPDATE or DELETE of `attempt` rows passes at the DB level. The app role is also the table owner. No concrete code path was found, so this is defense-in-depth only. The FR-38 guarantee 'XP is never reduced' rests on application code for TRUNCATE and on application code alone for the attempt log.
findings.suggestion: In a new migration (not an edit to V4 or V5), add a `BEFORE TRUNCATE` statement-level trigger for the ledger tables. Add the same UPDATE/DELETE trigger to `attempt`. Optionally add an `amount` check or trigger so that a REEVALUATION row can never reduce a task's total.

findings.title: Unpinned, floating base images and builder in Dockerfile and compose
findings.evidence: `postgres:16-alpine`, `maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21` and `eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine` are floating tags. A rebuild on the home laptop pulls whatever those tags point to at that moment, so builds are not reproducible. Accidental drift can also change the Postgres minor version used for the data volume. No dependency advisory scan was run (no network access in this review), so PDFBox 3.0.5 and the Spring Boot 4.1.1 transitives are unaudited.
findings.suggestion: Pin images by digest or at least by minor version. Run `mvn org.owasp:dependency-check-maven:check` or `npm audit` in CI and record the result before release.

findings.title: Practice/progress advice has no DataIntegrityViolationException handler (possible raw 500)
findings.evidence: V4/V5 add unique and foreign-key rules (attempt_task_scope_no_uq, xp_award_task_once_uq, xp_award_bonus_once_uq, ON DELETE RESTRICT on task_id). Only ContentProblemAdvice maps DataIntegrityViolationException (-> 409), and it is scoped to the content controllers. PracticeProblemAdvice and AdminStatsProblemAdvice map no integrity violation. Attempt races are serialised by pg_advisory_xact_lock in JdbcPracticeStore.kt:38, so the unique constraints should not be hit in practice. I did not trace the report/re-evaluation paths (xp_award_reevaluation_once_uq, attempt_reevaluation PK) or a task deleted concurrently with a play-through. If a constraint does fire there, the generic handler returns 500 or a non-contract problem.
findings.suggestion: Add a DataIntegrityViolationException -> 409/problem+json handler to the practice and stats advices. Or confirm that every write path that can hit these constraints takes the advisory lock. Add an IT for a concurrent double submit and a concurrent re-evaluation.

findings.title: V6 MISSION_BONUS shape check is loose (report_id/attempt_id)
findings.evidence: The check is `kind = 'MISSION_BONUS' AND task_id IS NULL AND (report_id IS NULL OR attempt_id IS NULL)`. It also allows a bonus with both report_id and attempt_id NULL. V5 documents that case only for a bonus credited when a mission is published already complete (OQ-28). The ledger rules therefore rest on application code, not the schema. The REEVALUATION and TASK shapes are strict.
findings.suggestion: Keep it if intended. Otherwise document the allowed combinations in a comment or the spec, or tighten them in a new migration (never edit V6).

findings.title: Operator backup excludes the doucko-storage volume
findings.evidence: `npm run backup` runs pg_dump only. Uploaded PDFs and task images live on the doucko-storage volume (compose.yaml). After a restore, task_image/source rows can point at files that no longer exist. restore.mjs prints a notice about this. compose.yaml says the same: 'npm run backup dumps only the database'. If NFR-10 requires the whole app data to be recoverable, this is partial.
findings.suggestion: Confirm NFR-10 covers only the database. If it covers uploads too, add a storage-volume archive step to backup/restore. Otherwise record the exclusion in the spec.

findings.title: pom 'no-sibling-contract' profile can silently skip codegen when ../docs is absent
findings.evidence: The profile sets codegen.skip=true when ../docs/api/openapi.yaml is missing. Its comment says it is for 'Phase 0/1 only'. The pinned-contract profile re-enables codegen only when contract/api/openapi.yaml exists. A checkout whose contract submodule is not initialised, in a directory without a sibling ../docs (CI or a worktree), will skip generation. The build then fails on missing *Api interfaces. It does not fail with a message pointing at the cause.
findings.suggestion: Remove the Phase 0/1 profile now that the contract is pinned. Or fail fast with an enforcer rule when contract/api/openapi.yaml is absent.

findings.title: Tools address only project doucko-e2e; owner project guard verified (no defect)
findings.evidence: assertE2eProject refuses every project name except 'doucko-e2e'. e2eComposeArgs always passes -p, both compose files and the committed fake env file. COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME, COMPOSE_FILE and the credentials are blocked from the process environment. `down -v` is therefore confined to the throwaway project. compose.e2e.yaml publishes only 127.0.0.1:18082 via !override, and e2e-stack.mjs re-checks the rendered ports. Committed secrets in tools/e2e-stack.env are labelled fake test values. Compose and migrations raised no cross-module or answer-key issue. The default `name: doucko` in compose.yaml is correct for the owner stack. backup.mjs and restore.mjs deliberately address the owner project (restore requires --yes and takes a safety backup first).
findings.suggestion: No action. Retain the OperatorToolGuardTest coverage.

findings.title: Attempt log has no database-level append-only guard, unlike xp_award and attempt_reevaluation
findings.evidence: The V4 header says the attempt log is append-only (FR-42, OQ-20) and 'Rows are only ever inserted'. Nothing enforces it in the database. V5 gives xp_award a BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE trigger and V6 gives attempt_reevaluation the same. `attempt` only has the (task_id, scope, attempt_no) unique constraint, so the guarantee depends on application code alone. The attempt table is also the evidence for XP and re-evaluation. The `attempt_id` foreign keys use ON DELETE RESTRICT, which blocks deletes of referenced rows but not UPDATEs, so `correct` or `parts` can still be changed in place. I could not run `git diff` because Bash is disabled, so I read the files directly. I did not check whether any application code updates `attempt`.
findings.suggestion: Add a new migration (V7, never edit V4) with a BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE trigger on `attempt`, modelled on `xp_award_append_only`. Optionally add BEFORE TRUNCATE statement triggers on attempt, xp_award and attempt_reevaluation, because row-level triggers do not fire on TRUNCATE.

findings.title: Deleting a mission cascades to practice_run while attempt, xp_award and opened_hint keep the mission id with no foreign key
findings.evidence: `practice_run.mission_id` is `REFERENCES mission(id) ON DELETE CASCADE`, but `attempt`, `opened_hint`, `problem_report` and `xp_award` carry `mission_id` with no foreign key by design, so the log outlives the mission. Deleting a mission therefore silently removes its replay-run rows and leaves the attempts, hints and XP rows pointing at it. The V4 header says 'the log outlives later mission edits'. Whether the application ever deletes missions, rather than unpublishing them, is not visible from these files.
findings.suggestion: Confirm that missions are never hard-deleted once practice data exists. If they can be, change the FK to ON DELETE RESTRICT or drop it, as is done for the other tables, in a new migration.

result.reasoning: The factual claim holds. V4__practice.sql line 4 says "Rows are only ever inserted: the attempt log is append-only (FR-42, OQ-20)", but it defines no trigger. V5 (xp_award) and V6 (attempt_reevaluation) do add refusal triggers. No other migration guards attempt or opened_hint. A grep of src found no production code that runs UPDATE or DELETE on attempt or opened_hint, so nothing is broken today. The gap is a missing defense-in-depth guard, not a live bug. Two parts of the finding are wrong or incomplete. Its title lumps in problem_report, but that table's status column (OPEN/FIXED/DISMISSED) has to be updatable, so it can't be made append-only. Also, ContentAuthoringIT.kt:53-54 runs `DELETE FROM attempt` and `DELETE FROM opened_hint` for test cleanup, so the suggested trigger would break those tests unless they switch to TRUNCATE or the migration allows for them. Keep it as a minor, low-confidence hardening suggestion, scoped to attempt and opened_hint.

The factual part holds. V4 has no trigger on attempt, opened_hint or problem_report, while V5 and V6 add one for xp_award and attempt_reevaluation. But nothing is exploitable or reproducible. In the practice module, the only UPDATE statements are `practice_run SET finished_at` and `problem_report SET status`, both in JdbcPracticeStore.kt. No code path updates or deletes attempt or opened_hint. No child or admin endpoint can reach such a statement, and my search covered only the practice module's Kotlin code, not other modules or the test sources. The finding's own evidence needs a "stray UPDATE" from some future bug or manual SQL, which is a defense-in-depth wish, not a defect a user or attacker can trigger. It also wrongly lumps in problem_report, which is mutable by design (status changes OPEN to something else). I found no requirement that mandates a DB-level guard for attempt (the V4 header only says rows are only inserted). A hardening suggestion with low confidence and no reproducible trigger does not count as a real problem.

The finding holds. V5__gamification.sql:37-39 declares `BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE ON xp_award FOR EACH ROW`. PostgreSQL does not fire row-level triggers on TRUNCATE, and there is no `BEFORE TRUNCATE` statement trigger or REVOKE TRUNCATE on this table in the code I read. The repo's own tests show the gap: PracticeTestSupport.kt:164-167, GamificationIT.kt:707 and ContentAuthoringIT.kt:51 run `TRUNCATE xp_award, rank_celebration, attempt_reevaluation`. PracticeTestSupport.kt:164 says the tables "refuse DELETE ... so they are truncated", so TRUNCATE succeeds on both xp_award and attempt_reevaluation. I did not open V6, but those tests cover attempt_reevaluation too. Severity "minor" fits: TRUNCATE needs DB-level privileges, and no application code path issues it, so user input cannot reach it. It is still a gap in the FR-38 guard.

The mechanism is real: the trigger at V5__gamification.sql:37-39 is a row-level BEFORE UPDATE OR DELETE trigger, and Postgres doesn't fire row-level triggers on TRUNCATE. Tests already run "TRUNCATE xp_award, rank_celebration, attempt_reevaluation" without the trigger refusing (ContentAuthoringIT.kt:51, PracticeTestSupport.kt:167, GamificationIT.kt:707). But there is no real-user or attacker path. No production code issues TRUNCATE, and running it needs table-owner or TRUNCATE privilege, so that actor could also drop the trigger. The gap only weakens defense-in-depth against operator or migration mistakes. Adding a BEFORE TRUNCATE trigger would break the existing test cleanups, so they would need rework. I did not read V6; the attempt_reevaluation claim is probably the same.

The mechanism is real: backup.mjs only runs pg_dump and does not touch the doucko-storage volume, and restore.mjs:113-114 prints a notice that files are not restored. But it is not a correctness defect. NFR-10 (contract/docs/requirements.md:171) requires only a pg_dump-based `npm run backup` and Postgres data surviving container restarts. It does not mention file storage. The limitation is a deliberate, documented scope decision, recorded in docs/qa/evidence/fix-restore-schema-drift.md and docs/current-state.md:106, and restore explicitly warns the operator. The claim that the operator gets no notice is false. This would be a requirements extension, not a bug in the code.

The mechanism is real. backup.mjs runs only pg_dump. restore.mjs prints that files on the doucko-storage volume are not restored. The storage keys in the DB would then point at missing files if the volume is lost. NFR-10 as written only requires a pg_dump-based backup of Postgres data, so this is not a spec violation. The gap is known and documented. It only bites when the storage volume is lost while the DB dump is restored, and it is operator-triggered, so it is not attacker-exploitable. It is a real limitation, but minor, as the finding says.

The core mechanism is real. tools/restore.mjs never stops the backend. After the safety backup (lines 88-97), it runs DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE and the replay in one transaction (lines 99-106). The backend is only restarted afterwards, and only if the restored schema is behind the expected migration version (lines 194-216). So a write committed between the safety backup and the swap is in neither the safety backup nor the restored data. Requests during the swap also contend with the DROP's exclusive locks. Pooled backend connections can hit a schema that has just been recreated, so that part of the claim holds.

The finding overstates the harm. A restore deliberately replaces all current data with the dump, so anything written after the dump is discarded by design, not by a race. Only the few seconds between the safety backup and the swap are actually unprotected. That window is narrow for a single-family tutor app, and the operator chose to run the restore. Calling it the data loss FR-31/FR-38 forbid is too strong, because those requirements cover normal operation, not an explicit destructive restore. The fix, stopping the backend or documenting an idle stack, is reasonable hardening.

tools/restore.mjs does not stop the backend before the swap. The safety backup (lines 89-93) runs first, then DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE and the replay run in one transaction (lines 99-106). A write the running backend commits between the safety backup and the swap is in neither the safety backup nor the dump, and requests during the swap block on ACCESS EXCLUSIVE locks or hit the new schema. The impact is narrow: restore intentionally discards all current data, so only the seconds-wide gap is an unintended loss. The tool is manual, operator-run, on a small single-family stack, and the failures are transient. Not reproduced by running it. Confirmed as a minor gap; keep minor.

The mechanism isn't reachable in practice. `MissionService.delete` (MissionService.kt:94-99) calls `MissionRules.missionDelete(usage.usedTasks(stored.content.taskIds))`. It refuses the delete with a Used conflict if any of the mission's tasks has an attempt, opened_hint or problem_report row (see `JdbcPracticeStore.usedTasks`). The `ON DELETE CASCADE` on `practice_run.mission_id` therefore only fires for missions whose tasks have no practice data. A replay run can only start after the primary play-through, which leaves attempts, so such runs belong to missions that can't be deleted. Any run the cascade does remove has no attempts or hints that could be orphaned. `practice_run` also holds no history of its own beyond mission_id, started_at and finished_at. The claimed state, replay-scope attempts whose run row no longer exists, would need a used task to be detached from the mission and the mission then deleted. That is an exotic edge the finding doesn't show and I didn't trace. There is a minor inconsistency in the comment: the header says "No foreign key on mission_id", yet `practice_run` has one. It has no runtime consequence, and the delete guard already enforces the intended behaviour at the application level.

The orphaning scenario can't happen through normal use. `MissionService.delete` (MissionService.kt:94-99) calls `MissionRules.missionDelete(usage.usedTasks(...))` and refuses with a conflict if any of the mission's tasks has an attempt, opened hint or problem report. `JdbcPracticeStore.usedTasks` (line 167) checks exactly those three tables. A replay run only produces attempts for tasks in the mission, so a mission with run history is blocked from deletion. The cascade therefore only removes runs that have no attempts, which orphans nothing. The mission-delete guard in the application layer is the reason the `ON DELETE CASCADE` on `practice_run` is harmless. A leftover edge case remains: an admin removes a used task from a mission, then deletes the mission. That is narrow and speculative, and the finding doesn't claim it. The finding is a consistency nit and not a reproducible defect.

The finding's claimed mechanism is wrong. .env.example sets DOUCKO_BIND_ADDRESS=127.0.0.1, not empty. Compose's ${VAR:-default} also substitutes the default when the variable is set but empty, so empty gives 127.0.0.1. The cited line is wrong (the port mapping is at compose.yaml:68). The only exposure path is an operator explicitly setting 0.0.0.0 and then bypassing the documented wrapper (documented in compose.yaml and .env.example). The suggested ':?' form only forces the variable to be set and does not block 0.0.0.0, so it adds no protection.

compose.yaml uses ${DOUCKO_BIND_ADDRESS:-127.0.0.1}. The ':-' form defaults when the variable is unset OR empty, so an empty value binds loopback. .env.example sets 127.0.0.1, not empty. The only bypass is an operator explicitly writing 0.0.0.0 into .env and running plain 'docker compose up', and that gap is already documented in compose.yaml and .env.example. Only the frontend 8081 is published; the backend and DB stay on the Compose network. The claimed empty-placeholder exposure does not occur.

The finding is speculative and I couldn't confirm a failure mechanism. compose.yaml:56 does use `wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/actuator/health | grep -q UP`, and the Dockerfile's runtime stage is `eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine`. But Alpine ships busybox wget by default, so the tool exists. Tomcat binds the wildcard address, which is dual-stack on a JVM, so it accepts connections on both 127.0.0.1 and ::1. Whichever address `localhost` resolves to first, the healthcheck connects. This `wget localhost:8080/actuator/health` pattern is a common one for Spring Boot on Alpine. The finding itself says "may" and "if it fails", gives no evidence of an actual failure, and is rated low confidence. The suggestion to use 127.0.0.1 is harmless hardening, not a correctness defect.

The healthcheck at compose.yaml:56 does use `wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/actuator/health | grep -q UP` on eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine (Dockerfile:11). The finding gives no mechanism for how it fails. Alpine ships the busybox wget applet, so the tool exists. Spring Boot's embedded Tomcat binds the wildcard address, which accepts both IPv4 and IPv6 loopback, so `localhost` resolves and connects whichever address is tried first. The known `localhost`/`::1` failure affects services that bind IPv4 only, such as nginx, and not this backend. The finding only says it "may" resolve to ::1 first and "if it fails". I could not confirm a real failure, and the evidence is speculative. At most this is a hardening suggestion, not a reproducible defect.

The mechanism is real. compose.yaml:68 publishes `${DOUCKO_BIND_ADDRESS:-127.0.0.1}:8081:80` with no interpolation guard. The loopback/RFC 1918 check runs only in `npm run stack:up`, and the compose.yaml header comment (lines 1-3) says a plain `docker compose up` skips it. The backend doesn't close the gap. The Host allowlist in SecurityConfiguration.kt:50 accepts localhost, `backend`, or any IPv4 literal, so a request to a public IP would pass it. Exploiting this takes a deliberate misconfiguration: the owner has to set 0.0.0.0 or a public address in .env and bypass the wrapper. The admin login is also still password-protected. This is a documented defense-in-depth gap, so I'm keeping the severity at minor.

The mechanism is real, but it needs the owner to set the value. The frontend port is `${DOUCKO_BIND_ADDRESS:-127.0.0.1}:8081:80` (compose.yaml:68; the finding cites line 60, which is the backend `restart` line). A plain `docker compose up` does not run the loopback/RFC 1918 check in tools/stack.mjs. Compose has no interpolation validation for this value, so 0.0.0.0 would be published. The backend and db publish no ports. An outside attacker cannot trigger this. The default is loopback, and the owner has to put a public address in .env and bypass `stack:up`. Even then the exposure is only the admin login, which is still password-protected (ADMIN_PASSWORD of at least 12 characters, NFR-16). The comment in compose.yaml documents the gap, and earlier review runs already raised it. It is a defense-in-depth gap against owner misconfiguration, not an exploitable vulnerability, so I downgrade it.

tools/restore.mjs never stops the backend before the DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE (lines 99-106). It restarts the backend only when the restored Flyway version is behind the target (line 194). A write between the safety backup and the drop is therefore in neither the safety backup nor the restored dump. Pooled connections and cached statements also stay attached to the replaced schema when versions match, because no restart happens. Nothing in the file or its callers guards against this, and the header comment doesn't mention it. The practical impact is small: it is an operator-run tool for a single-family deployment, and the restore replaces all data anyway. The 'security' dimension label is also wrong, since this is a correctness and robustness issue. Minor severity is appropriate.

The mechanism is real, but the impact is smaller than the finding claims. In tools/restore.mjs the only `compose` calls before the drop are read-only queries (`exec psql`, `ps`). Nothing stops or pauses the backend. Line 104 runs `DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE` in a single psql transaction while the backend can still serve. The only gap is a narrow edge: a task is removed from a mission by editing it, and the mission is deleted afterwards. In that case old `attempt.mission_id` values could dangle. But that is the 'log outlives later mission edits' behaviour the header describes, and the finding doesn't claim it. The finding itself is low confidence and admits it can't see whether deletes happen.

The finding doesn't hold up as a real problem. Missions can be hard-deleted (DELETE /api/admin/missions/{id} → MissionService.delete), but a guard sits in front of it. MissionService.kt:97 refuses the delete with a conflict if any task in the mission has an attempt, opened_hint or problem_report row (JdbcPracticeStore.usedTasks, line 167). So a delete only goes through when the mission's tasks have no practice data. In that case only empty or abandoned practice_run rows cascade, and no attempt, hint or XP rows can be left pointing at the mission. The V4 header says the lack of a mission_id FK is deliberate, so the log can outlive mission edits. The only gap I could find is a narrow edge case. A used task could first be edited out of a mission, and the mission could then be deleted. The attempts would keep a mission_id with no mission, which is what the no-FK design intends, and they are still tied to their task by a RESTRICT FK. The finding itself says low confidence and minor severity. It is not exploitable by an attacker, since the endpoint is admin-only, and it has no user-visible impact.
